lessons.title: Risk management and data governance
lessons.subtitle: Why the risk file never closes, and why weak training data turns into the expensive problem
keyConcepts: Risk-management system as an iterative process (Article 9)
Special-category data exception for bias correction (Article 10(5))

sections.title: The risk-management system is never finished
sections.content:
**From here on, the material is for people who work with AI systems professionally or answer for them.**

Reading as a member of the public, for the framework and your own rights? Blocks 1 and 2 were the whole story. Blocks 3 to 6 are for whoever buys, runs, or signs off on an AI system.

---

A risk-management system is not a document. Article 9(1) asks for one that is **established, implemented, documented, and maintained**. The last word is the expensive one: a continuous, iterative process across the whole lifecycle, systematically reviewed and updated (Article 9(2)).

**Four required steps** (Article 9(2), points (a) to (d)):

- **(a) Identify and analyse** known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety, and fundamental rights.
- **(b) Estimate and evaluate** risks that may emerge under reasonably foreseeable misuse.
- **(c) Evaluate** other risks identified through post-market monitoring under Article 72.
- **(d) Adopt** appropriate and targeted risk-management measures.

**Hierarchy of measures** (Article 9(5), second subparagraph): design the risk out first, then mitigate and control, then inform and train under Article 13 for what is left. Testing before the system is placed on the market or put into service is mandatory (Article 9(8)). The likely impact on people under 18 has to be weighed explicitly (Article 9(9)).

**Practical implementation for SMEs:** one risk matrix, carrying the risk, its likelihood, its severity, the control, the owner, and the model version. Set a review interval that fits the system; quarterly suits a system that keeps moving, and the Regulation does not prescribe that interval. Findings from post-market monitoring under Article 72 flow back into the matrix. Infringements of the requirements or obligations listed in Article 99(4) can attract fines of up to EUR 15 million or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, subject to the conditions and calculation rules in Article 99.
sections.keyTakeaway: Four required steps run across the whole lifecycle. Identify and analyse, estimate and evaluate, weigh the post-market findings, adopt targeted measures. A risk-management system nobody has touched since roll-out does not satisfy Article 9.

sections.title: Data governance: eight required elements in Article 10
sections.content:
Your training data is evidence. Training, validation, and testing data sets carry their own quality criteria (Article 10(1)); for systems built without model training, the criteria bite only on testing data sets (Article 10(6)).

**Eight practices to address and document** (Article 10(2), points (a) to (h)):

- (a) relevant design choices
- (b) data-collection processes and the origin of data; for personal data, the original purpose of collection
- (c) relevant data-preparation operations, including annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment, and aggregation
- (d) assumptions about what the data is intended to measure and represent
- (e) assessment of the availability, quantity, and suitability of the data sets
- (f) examination of possible biases that may affect health, safety, fundamental rights, or lead to discrimination prohibited under Union law
- (g) appropriate measures to detect, prevent, and mitigate those biases
- (h) identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings and how they can be addressed

Data sets must be **relevant, sufficiently representative, and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete** (Article 10(3)). They must also reflect the geographical, contextual, behavioural, or functional setting the system is intended for (Article 10(4)).

**Practical implementation for SMEs:** one data sheet per data set, along the lines of Annex IV, point 2(d): source, acquisition method, size, principal characteristics, labelling, cleaning steps. A set pulled from Hugging Face or Kaggle gets the same sheet as one you collected yourself. Without provenance and preparation records, the technical documentation and the conformity assessment have a hole in them.
sections.keyTakeaway: One data sheet per data set, covering all eight elements in Article 10(2). Bought data is held to the same standard as your own.

sections.title: Special-category data for bias correction and the GDPR link
sections.content:
Measuring bias sometimes takes the very data Article 9 GDPR keeps locked. Article 10(5) opens a narrow door: special categories of personal data, such as data revealing racial or ethnic origin, health data, or religious beliefs, may be processed to detect and correct bias. Only where that is strictly necessary, and only where other data, synthetic or anonymised included, cannot achieve the objective effectively.

**Six cumulative conditions** (Article 10(5), points (a) to (f)). Miss one and the legal basis is gone:

- (a) the bias cannot be detected and corrected effectively by processing other data
- (b) the special-category data is subject to technical limitations on reuse and state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
- (c) the data is secured, protected, subject to access controls, and accessible only to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations
- (d) the data is not transmitted, transferred, or otherwise accessed by other parties
- (e) the data is deleted once the bias has been corrected or the retention period for personal data ends, whichever occurs first
- (f) the records of processing under Article 30 GDPR include the reasons why processing was strictly necessary and why the objective could not be achieved with other data

Bias can also be exploited deliberately for data-poisoning attacks (BSI white paper *Bias in AI*, July 2025). Detection can use variance and subgroup analysis; mitigation may come before, during, or after model training.

**Practical implementation for SMEs:** you want to test your recruitment system for sex-related bias, which takes data about sex. Article 10(5) carries that, but only with every condition met and documented. Bring in the data protection officer where the GDPR requires it, and keep the Article 30 record with the strict-necessity reasoning inside it. Article 10(5) does not name consent as an extra condition. The door stays narrow anyway, and the rest of data-protection law still applies.

Name someone for AI risk management, even though the Regulation does not prescribe that job title. A name, a role, a start date: the first Article 9 control you can actually show an auditor.
sections.keyTakeaway: Special-category data for bias work only when all six conditions in Article 10(5) hold at once. Bring in the data protection officer, and put the strict-necessity reasoning into the Article 30 GDPR record.

quiz.questionText: Which statement about the risk-management system under Article 9 of the AI Act is correct?

answerOptions.text: A one-off risk analysis before placing the system on the market is sufficient if it is archived.
It is a continuous, iterative process throughout the lifecycle, with regular systematic review and updating (Article 9(2)).
It is required only when the high-risk AI system is a safety component of a product listed in Annex I.
It is the responsibility of the notified body, not the provider.

quiz.explanation: Article 9(2) says it plainly: a continuous, iterative process across the entire lifecycle, systematically reviewed and updated. Findings from post-market monitoring under Article 72 feed back into it. The duty sits with the provider, not with the notified body.

quiz.questionText: Which measure does Article 10(2) NOT expressly require for training, validation, and testing data sets?

answerOptions.text: Data-preparation operations such as annotation, labelling, and cleaning (Article 10(2), point (c))
Examination of possible biases that may lead to prohibited discrimination (Article 10(2), point (f))
A statement of the training data's carbon footprint
Identification of data gaps and shortcomings, and how they can be addressed (Article 10(2), point (h))

quiz.explanation: Article 10(2) lists eight practices in points (a) to (h). A carbon-footprint statement is not one of them. Energy-consumption information belongs to the technical documentation for GPAI models in Annex XI, not to Article 10.

quiz.questionText: When may a provider process special categories of personal data, such as data revealing ethnic origin, to detect and correct bias?

answerOptions.text: Whenever a high-risk system is trained and there is a suspicion of bias.
Only when all six conditions in Article 10(5), points (a) to (f), are met cumulatively and other data cannot achieve the objective effectively.
Only with the express written consent of every data subject.
Only after a notified body has approved the processing.

quiz.explanation: Article 10(5) is a narrow exception for processing special categories of personal data. All six safeguards have to hold at once: no effective alternative, technical limits and privacy-preserving measures, access control, no access by other parties, timely deletion, and an Article 30 GDPR record explaining strict necessity. Article 10(5) does not name consent as an extra condition, and the other applicable GDPR duties stay in force.

lessons.title: Technical documentation and logs
lessons.subtitle: What Annex IV asks for, and why your system needs a flight recorder
keyConcepts: Annex IV as the minimum documentation structure
Retention: 10 years for provider records, at least 6 months for deployer logs

sections.title: Annex IV: what the technical documentation must contain
sections.content:
The market surveillance authority asks for the technical documentation. What you hand over is the central piece of evidence: drawn up **before the system is placed on the market or put into service**, kept up to date from then on (Article 11(1)).

**SME simplification** (Article 11(1), second subparagraph): microenterprises and small and medium-sized enterprises may supply the elements of Annex IV in simplified form, through a Commission form that notified bodies must accept. Simplified means shorter, not thinner. Every required subject stays in.

**Nine main parts of Annex IV:**

- (1) a general description, including intended purpose, provider, version, and forms of distribution
- (2) a detailed description of the system and development process, including methods, architecture, data requirements, human oversight, validation, and cybersecurity
- (3) detailed information about monitoring, functioning, and control, including accuracy for relevant persons or groups
- (4) the appropriateness of performance metrics
- (5) the risk-management system under Article 9
- (6) relevant changes through the lifecycle
- (7) harmonised standards and other specifications applied
- (8) a copy of the EU declaration of conformity
- (9) the post-market monitoring plan under Article 72

**Practical implementation for SMEs:** Article 18(1) makes providers keep the documentation listed there for 10 years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service. Take the simplified form where it exists and applies. And version the documentation like source code, release by release, in a repository that keeps an audit trail.
sections.keyTakeaway: Nine areas from Annex IV, simplified through the SME form under Article 11(1) where that applies, kept 10 years under Article 18, versioned with every relevant release.

sections.title: Automatic recording: event logs under Article 12
sections.content:
A flight recorder is not retrofitted. Article 12(1) makes automatic event recording a **design requirement**: the high-risk system must technically allow events relevant to identifying risk situations and substantial modifications to be recorded over its lifetime.

**Purposes of the logs** (Article 12(2)): identifying situations that may create a risk under Article 79(1) or constitute a substantial modification; facilitating post-market monitoring under Article 72; and monitoring operation under Article 26(5).

**Minimum logging capabilities for remote biometric identification systems** listed in Annex III, point 1(a) (Article 12(3), points (a) to (d)):

- (a) the period of each use, including the start and end date and time
- (b) the reference database against which input data was checked
- (c) the input data for which a match resulted
- (d) the identification of the natural persons involved in verifying the results under Article 14(5)

**Retention by the deployer:** at least **six months** (Article 26(6)), unless applicable Union or national law, including data-protection law, provides otherwise.

**Practical implementation for SMEs:** machine-readable logs, filled automatically, exportable for the market surveillance authority, covering the events the legal purposes and this system actually need. Append-only helps: a log that can be edited afterwards is worth little as evidence. Article 12 prescribes no product and no storage architecture; SIEM tooling such as Splunk, the Elastic Stack, or Wazuh is one proportionate option.
sections.keyTakeaway: Logging is a design duty under Article 12. Remote biometric identification carries four specified capabilities. Deployers keep logs under their control for at least six months, subject to other applicable law.

sections.title: Provider and deployer: who documents what
sections.content:
The duties split by role. The line only blurs once a deployer changes the system.

**Provider** (Articles 11, 18, 19, and 47):

- prepares the Annex IV technical documentation before the system is placed on the market or put into service
- keeps logs automatically generated by the system to the extent they are under the provider's control (Article 19)
- keeps the EU declaration of conformity for 10 years (Article 47(1))

**Deployer** (Article 26(5) and (6)):

- monitors the system's operation on the basis of the instructions for use
- keeps automatically generated logs under its control for at least six months, unless other applicable law provides otherwise
- follows the reporting and cooperation duties that apply when it identifies a risk or serious incident; provider reporting deadlines are set out in Article 73 and vary by circumstance

**Change of role** (Article 25): a person that makes a **substantial modification** to a high-risk system or changes its intended purpose in a way covered by Article 25 may become the provider, with the matching documentation and conformity-assessment duties. Fine-tuning or retraining is not automatically a substantial modification in every case; assess it against the definition in Article 3(23), the planned changes identified by the original provider, and Article 25.

**Practical implementation for SMEs:** buy a recruitment product, run it as supplied, and you are the deployer. Fine-tune it on your own applicant data or change its intended purpose, and you owe a documented Article 25 assessment. Is the change substantial within the Regulation? Then the provider duties follow, Annex IV documentation and conformity assessment included. The cost difference is not small.
sections.keyTakeaway: Provider: the Annex IV documentation, plus 10 years for the specified provider records. Deployer: the logs under its control for at least six months. A deployer becomes a provider only where the Article 25 conditions are met, and fine-tuning does not settle that on its own.

quiz.questionText: What must the technical documentation for a high-risk AI system contain at a minimum?

answerOptions.text: A two-page summary of the business model and target market.
The nine main areas in Annex IV, kept up to date (Article 11(1) read with Annex IV).
Only the EU declaration of conformity under Annex V.
Only a copy of the instructions for use under Article 13.

quiz.explanation: Annex IV sets the minimum structure: a general description; system elements and development process; monitoring, functioning, and control; performance metrics; the risk-management system; lifecycle changes; standards; the declaration of conformity; and the post-market monitoring plan. SMEs may use the simplified Commission form under Article 11(1), second subparagraph. The required subject matter stays the same.

quiz.questionText: For how long must a deployer keep automatically generated logs of a high-risk AI system that are under its control?

answerOptions.text: For 24 hours after use ends.
For at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise (Article 26(6)).
For 10 years after the system is placed on the market, matching the EU declaration of conformity.
Until the system's next major update.

quiz.explanation: Article 26(6) sets a floor of six months for logs under the deployer's control, unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise. Data-protection requirements can pull that period down; other legal duties can push it up. The 10 years in Article 47(1) belong to the provider's EU declaration of conformity.

quiz.questionText: A company fine-tunes a purchased AI recruitment tool using its own applicant data. What is the correct role assessment?

answerOptions.text: It always remains only a deployer because fine-tuning is legally irrelevant.
It must assess whether the change is a substantial modification under Article 25; if it is, the company becomes the provider and assumes the relevant documentation and conformity-assessment duties.
It becomes an importer within the meaning of Article 23.
It is responsible only for logs, never for technical documentation.

quiz.explanation: Article 25 changes the role once its conditions are met, including where a person makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system. Fine-tuning can matter here, but it is not automatically a substantial modification in every case. Assess the change against Article 3(23), the provider's predetermined changes, the intended purpose, and Article 25.

lessons.title: Human oversight, accuracy, and cybersecurity
lessons.subtitle: The stop control, the second pair of eyes, and the attacks aimed at your model
keyConcepts: Two-person verification for remote biometric identification (Article 14(5))
Accuracy and robustness as design requirements (Article 15)

sections.title: Human oversight: from the concept to the stop control
sections.content:
Who presses stop? Article 14(1) wants that answered in the design: high-risk AI systems must be built so natural persons can effectively oversee them while they are in use. Oversight is a **design requirement**, not aftercare.

**Two sources of oversight measures** (Article 14(3)):

- (a) measures identified and, when technically feasible, built into the system by the provider before it is placed on the market or put into service, such as interface controls, confidence information, or a stop function
- (b) measures identified by the provider that the deployer is expected to implement, such as roles, training, and escalation paths

**Five oversight capabilities** (Article 14(4), points (a) to (e)) that the oversight measures must enable, as appropriate and proportionate:

- (a) **understand** the system's relevant capacities and limitations and detect anomalies
- (b) remain **aware of automation bias**, particularly when the output informs decisions made by natural persons
- (c) **interpret** the output correctly, taking the available interpretation tools and methods into account
- (d) **decide not to use** the system or disregard, override, or reverse its output
- (e) **intervene in operation or stop the system** through a stop control or comparable safe procedure

**Independent verification** (Article 14(5)): for remote biometric identification systems listed in Annex III, point 1(a), no action or decision may be taken on the basis of an identification unless at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training, and authority have separately verified and confirmed it. The paragraph carries a proportionate exception for certain law-enforcement, migration, border-control, and asylum systems where Union or national law treats the requirement as disproportionate.

**Practical implementation for SMEs:** the oversight interface carries what the risk demands, from a visible stop route to confidence information per output and trained people (Article 4, block 2). Remote biometric identification at a site entrance: a match opens no door on its own, and where Article 14(5) applies, two people confirm it separately.
sections.keyTakeaway: Human oversight means the five capabilities in Article 14(4), built in a form appropriate and proportionate to the system. For remote biometric identification, Article 14(5) generally puts two qualified people between the match and the action.

sections.title: Accuracy and resilience: what an appropriate level means
sections.content:
Appropriate is not a soft word. Article 15(1) requires an **appropriate level** of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity across the whole lifecycle, and Article 8(1) ties that to the generally acknowledged state of the art. Harmonised standards published under Article 40 can create a presumption of conformity for the requirements they cover.

**Metrics in the instructions for use** (Article 15(3)): the provider declares the levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics in the accompanying instructions. No metric, no oversight.

**Resilience** (Article 15(4)): the system must be as resilient as possible to errors, faults, or inconsistencies, inside the system or in the environment it operates in. Technical redundancy can mean backup models or fail-safe paths. Where a system keeps learning after it is placed on the market or put into service, feedback loops, meaning possibly biased outputs that become future inputs, need appropriate mitigation measures.

**Practical implementation for SMEs:** set the performance criteria before release, with metrics and representative data that fit the intended purpose. Monitor performance and drift in operation, and wire a threshold breach into the post-market monitoring and corrective-action process under Article 72. A value such as F1 >= 0.85 is only an example; the Regulation does not set that universal threshold. Apply harmonised standards once published, and until then document the technical specifications and state-of-the-art basis you selected.
sections.keyTakeaway: Accuracy and resilience are lifecycle design duties. Set purpose-specific metrics before release, watch for drift, and record how the Article 72 process answers a threshold breach.

sections.title: Cybersecurity: four AI-specific attack classes
sections.content:
Your model is a target. Article 15(5) requires high-risk systems to be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs, or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities.

**Four AI-specific threats** expressly identified in the paragraph:

- **data poisoning**, meaning manipulation of the training data before or during training
- **model poisoning**, meaning manipulation of trained model components, including backdoors
- **adversarial examples or model evasion**, meaning crafted inputs that induce incorrect outputs
- **confidentiality attacks**, including model inversion or membership inference used to extract or infer training information

The BSI white paper *Bias in AI* (July 2025) shows that bias can be exploited deliberately in data-poisoning attacks. Bias controls and security controls are one subject, not two.

**Practical implementation for SMEs:** adversarial testing on a risk-based cadence, recorded with method, scope, findings, and remediation. Annual can be a sensible baseline for some systems, and Article 15 does not prescribe a universal interval. Open tooling exists, such as ART from IBM or CleverHans. For a third-party model, read the model card, check provenance, pin the version, record integrity hashes where they exist, and reassess when something material changes upstream. The testing and control evidence belongs in the technical documentation under Annex IV, point 2(g).
sections.keyTakeaway: Four attack classes: data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples or model evasion, confidentiality attacks. Test on a risk basis and document it. Article 15 does not prescribe one universal interval.

quiz.questionText: Which combination describes the five oversight capabilities in Article 14(4)?

answerOptions.text: Understand relevant capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, interpret output, disregard or override output, and intervene or stop the system.
Notify the provider, manager, data protection officer, works council, and IT team.
Read source code, debug the model, adjust hyperparameters, initiate retraining, and perform a rollback.
Read the documentation, complete training, keep a log, report an incident, and escalate to an AI officer.

quiz.explanation: Article 14(4), points (a) to (e), names exactly these capabilities as the threshold for effective oversight, with measures appropriate and proportionate to the risks, autonomy, and context. Notification chains and technical maintenance tasks matter day to day, but they are not the list in Article 14(4).

quiz.questionText: What does the separate-verification rule in Article 14(5) require?

answerOptions.text: Four people must approve every AI output before it can be used.

For remote biometric identification under Annex III, point 1(a), at least two competent, trained, and authorised natural persons must separately verify and confirm the identification before action is taken, subject to the stated exception.
The provider and deployer must each appoint two oversight officers.
Two people must purchase the system and two must maintain it.

quiz.explanation: Article 14(5) blocks action or decisions taken on an identification alone. At least two competent, trained, and authorised natural persons must separately verify and confirm it. The rule covers remote biometric identification under Annex III, point 1(a), and carries a proportionate exception for specified public-authority contexts.

quiz.questionText: Which attack is NOT one of the four AI-specific threats identified in Article 15(5)?

answerOptions.text: Data poisoning through manipulation of training data
Model poisoning through manipulation of trained model components
Email phishing directed at end users
Adversarial examples or model evasion

quiz.explanation: Article 15(5) names data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples or model evasion, and confidentiality attacks. Phishing goes after people, not the model. It stays a security problem, just not one under Article 15.

lessons.title: Conformity assessment and CE marking
lessons.subtitle: When a notified body, when internal control, and how a CE mark lands on an API
keyConcepts: Internal control (Annex VI) and notified-body assessment (Annex VII)
EU declaration of conformity retained for 10 years (Article 47)
Registration in the EU database (Articles 49 and 71)

sections.title: Which procedure applies? The decision logic in Article 43
sections.content:
Seven of the eight Annex III categories need no notified body at all. Which procedure applies is decided by the category (Article 43).

**Annex III, point 1 (biometrics):** where the provider has applied the harmonised standards under Article 40, or common specifications under Article 41, it may choose between internal control under Annex VI and assessment of its quality-management system and technical documentation by a notified body under Annex VII (Article 43(1)). The conditions in Article 43(1) decide when the notified-body route is required.

**Annex III, points 2 to 8** (critical infrastructure, education, employment, access to services, law enforcement, migration, and administration of justice): the provider follows internal control under Annex VI (Article 43(2)); that paragraph does not require a notified body.

**Sector-specific cases** (Article 43(3)): for systems tied to products covered by Annex I, section A, such as machinery, medical devices, motor vehicles, or toys, the sectoral conformity-assessment procedure absorbs the AI Act requirements.

**Internal control (Annex VI):** the provider verifies the quality-management system under Article 17, examines the technical documentation, and checks that design, development, and post-market monitoring are consistent with it. No third party checks first; the responsibility stays with the provider.

**Notified body (Annex VII):** the body assesses the quality-management system and technical documentation and carries out surveillance. It may obtain access to training, validation, and testing data, including through an API or other appropriate technical means. A certificate is valid for no more than four years for systems covered by Annex III (Article 44(2)).

**Practical implementation for SMEs:** recruitment AI (point 4), creditworthiness (point 5), and education systems (point 3) run through Annex VI under Article 43(2). For remote biometric identification under point 1(a), work the exact Article 43(1) conditions. Check a candidate notified body against the accreditation authority and the Commission's NANDO database.
sections.keyTakeaway: Annex III, point 1 runs on the Article 43(1) choice and its conditions. Points 2 to 8 run on internal control under Annex VI pursuant to Article 43(2).

sections.title: EU declaration of conformity and CE marking
sections.content:
**EU declaration of conformity** (Article 47):

- in writing, machine-readable, and signed physically or electronically
- kept by the provider for **10 years** after the system has been placed on the market or put into service (Article 47(1))
- content follows Annex V: system identification, a statement of conformity, applicable standards and specifications, provider details
- where several Union legal acts apply, one declaration may cover them all and must identify them

**CE marking** (Article 48):

- follows the general principles in Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 and is affixed visibly, legibly, and indelibly
- where that is impossible or unwarranted because of the system's nature, it goes on the packaging or accompanying documentation, as appropriate
- **digital CE marking** applies to systems supplied digitally and may be reached through the interface or an easily accessible machine-readable code or other electronic means (Article 48(2))
- where a notified body was involved, its identification number follows the CE marking (Article 48(4))

**Practical implementation for SMEs:** for SaaS, an API, or other digitally supplied software, put the CE marking and the declaration where Article 48 is satisfied, through the interface or another accessible route. Write down why that placement is visible and reachable for your delivery model. Incorrect or missing CE marking can amount to formal non-compliance under Article 83. Infringements of obligations listed in Article 99(5) can attract fines of up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% of total worldwide annual turnover, subject to the Regulation's calculation and proportionality rules.
sections.keyTakeaway: The EU declaration of conformity stays with the provider for 10 years under Article 47. CE marking goes on in the form Article 48 requires, digital route included for systems supplied digitally.

sections.title: Registration in the EU database under Articles 49 and 71
sections.content:
Registration comes before market entry. Once the relevant high-risk rules apply, providers of systems listed in Annex III register themselves and their system in the EU database under Article 71 **before placing the system on the market or putting it into service** (Article 49(1)). Systems covered by Annex III, point 2, are registered at national level (Article 49(5)).

A provider that concludes under Article 6(3) that an Annex III system is not high-risk is not off the hook: document the assessment, then check the registration requirement in the applicable text. Public-authority deployers and Union institutions, bodies, offices, or agencies deploying Annex III systems also carry registration duties under Article 49.

**Required information from Annex VIII, section A** includes provider details, trade name, intended purpose, system status, standards applied, a copy of the declaration of conformity, and electronic instructions for use.

The Commission is the controller of the EU database (Article 71(6)). The registered information is generally publicly accessible and machine-readable, and non-public sections exist for specified public-authority uses.

**Substantial modification** (Article 43(4)): a new conformity assessment may be required where a system already assessed is substantially modified.

**Timing:** check the registration and conformity-assessment requirements before each release, and record after every material update whether the analysis has changed. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, sets 2 December 2027 for stand-alone Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for systems embedded in products covered by Annex I.

**For deployers:** applying your own CE marking is not automatically your duty. Read the provider's documentation and EU declaration of conformity, and assess any change of role under Article 25.
sections.keyTakeaway: Covered Annex III systems are registered under Articles 49 and 71 before they are placed on the market or put into service. A substantial modification can trigger a new conformity assessment under Article 43(4). The amended high-risk dates are staged across 2027 and 2028.

quiz.questionText: An SME develops an AI recruitment system that is high-risk under Annex III, point 4(a). Which conformity-assessment procedure applies?

answerOptions.text: Assessment by a notified body under Annex VII, with a four-year certificate.
Internal control under Annex VI; Article 43(2) does not require a notified body.
A TÜV certification is mandatory regardless of the high-risk category.
Only registration in the EU database is required; there is no assessment procedure.

quiz.explanation: Article 43(2) prescribes internal control under Annex VI for high-risk systems listed in Annex III, points 2 to 8, and recruitment sits in point 4. A notified-body assessment becomes relevant for point 1 biometric systems, under the conditions in Article 43(1).

quiz.questionText: For how long must the provider keep the EU declaration of conformity for a high-risk AI system?

answerOptions.text: Six months, matching the deployer's log-retention period under Article 26(6).
Four years, matching the maximum validity of a notified body's certificate under Article 44(2).
10 years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service, with the declaration supplied to authorities on request (Article 47(1)).
Until the first substantial modification, after which the new declaration replaces every prior record.

quiz.explanation: Article 47(1) requires the provider to keep the declaration for 10 years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service, and to supply it to competent national authorities on request. Six months belongs to deployer logs under Article 26(6); four years is the maximum certificate validity in Article 44(2) for systems covered by Annex III.

quiz.questionText: Where is an Annex III high-risk AI system, other than one in point 2, registered before it is placed on the market or put into service?

answerOptions.text: With Germany's Federal Office for Information Security (BSI).
In the Commission's EU database under Article 71, using the information required by Annex VIII (Article 49(1)).
With the German Patent and Trade Mark Office (DPMA).
With the provider's local chamber of commerce.

quiz.explanation: Article 49(1) requires registration in the EU database under Article 71. The registered information is generally publicly accessible and machine-readable, and the Commission is the controller under Article 71(6). Annex III, point 2 systems go through national registration under Article 49(5).
